query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid quenching followed by controlled sub-critical annealing in an inert atmosphere produces a bimodal grain size distribution in refractory high‐entropy alloys that improves ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact‐induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high‐entropy alloy produced via standard methods (e.g., PBF-LB/M) exhibiting a single‐phase, relatively uniform grain structure with limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a heat-treatment schedule consisting of rapid quenching to lock in a fine-grained structure, then subject the alloy to controlled sub-critical annealing (below approximately 80% of the melting temperature) in an inert atmosphere to allow selective growth of some grains, resulting in a bimodal grain size distribution.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be conducted under an inert atmosphere, with annealing temperatures maintained below ~80% of the alloy’s melting point and with controlled cooling rates to balance between ultrafine and larger grain formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Bimodal grain size microstructure where ultrafine grains maintain high strength and energy-release characteristics while the larger grains enhance ductility and promote uniform deformability.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine grain regions increase resistance to dislocation movement to maintain high strength and rapid energy release, while the presence of larger, ductile grains allows for more uniform plastic deformation and improved ductility. This dual microstructure minimizes strain localization during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the thermally treated alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved ductility and uniform deformability with little to no reduction in strength or impact-induced energy release.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys with a uniform grain structure that typically display lower ductility and issues with strain localization under impact.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only when the processing conditions (inert atmosphere, controlled sub-critical annealing below ~80% Tm, and appropriate quenching rate) are strictly maintained. Excessive annealing or deviation from these parameters (e.g., exposure to reactive atmospheres) may lead to undesirable grain growth or oxidation, negating the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in ductility and the extent to which strength and energy-release properties are fully preserved remain to be determined and may depend on the exact processing parameters and alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory high-entropy alloy samples. One set undergoes the rapid quench and controlled sub-critical annealing treatment in an inert atmosphere, while the other set remains untreated. Perform microstructural characterization (e.g., via SEM/EBSD) to verify the formation of a bimodal grain size distribution in the treated set. Then conduct mechanical tests including tensile and impact-fracture experiments to assess ductility, strength, and impact-induced energy release.
measurements: Tensile strength and elongation at break
Impact-induced energy release or fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in ductility and uniform deformability, or if they exhibit a reduction in strength or diminished impact-induced energy release compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

AbstractThe excellent cryogenic tensile properties of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy are generally caused by deformation twinning, which is difficult to achieve at room temperature because of insufficient stress for twinning. Here, we induced twinning at room temperature to improve the cryogenic tensile properties of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy. Considering grain size effects on the critical stress for twinning, twins were readily formed in the coarse microstructure by cold rolling without grain refinement by hot rolling. These twins were retained by partial recrystallization and played an important role in improving strength, allowing yield strengths approaching 1 GPa. The persistent elongation up to 46% as well as the tensile strength of 1.3 GPa are attributed to additional twinning in both recrystallized and non-recrystallization regions. Our results demonstrate that non-recrystallized grains, which are generally avoided in conventional alloys because of their deleterious effect on ductility, can be useful in achieving high-strength high-entropy alloys.
